transcript:
Header:
Date/Time: 2026-08-12 15:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes (recording)
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (CTO, Horizon Analytics), Liam Chen (Platform Lead), Renee Ortiz (SRE)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Demo focused on edge cases: long context handling, high TPS load patterns, streaming backpressure behavior and timeouts.
- Covered batching, KV cache, quantization tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted routing, and security/compliance questions.
- Agreed to run a 48h pilot/benchmark; SE to share test config and Redwood to send pricing & security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: alright everyone, thanks for joining, uh we can kick off, I'm Jordan from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account, and with me is Maya our systems engineer, she'll do most of the deep dive.
[00:07] Aisha Khan: Hey thanks, appreciate it. Quick note we have limited time, we want to focus on the long context and high TPS behavior, and streaming behavior under backpressure.
[00:14] Jordan Lee: perfect, that's exactly what we prepared. Maya, wanna take it?
[00:17] Maya Patel: yeah thanks Jordan. so quick agenda, we'll run a short console walkthrough, show API examples for long context and streaming, then demo a synthetic high-TPS test and show how backpressure and timeouts surface, and finish with Q&A.
[00:29] Liam Chen: sounds good. on our side, our main constraints: 1) we have 1.2M tokens/day baseline, peaks to 6k rps for short bursts, 2) we need some requests to preserve a 200k token conversation context occasionally for multi-turn analytics, and 3) we need SOC2 and KMS-based key separation.
[00:47] Maya Patel: okay noted. on the context piece, we use prefix/KV cache to avoid re-sending the whole 200k tokens, there are limits and we can shard long contexts across streams. i'll demo how Redwood handles it with different quantization and KV cache configs.
[01:02] Renee Ortiz: hmm 200k token context, just to flag, that's larger than typical, how does latency behave?
[01:07] Maya Patel: good question. latency depends on whether the model is warm and whether you're using streaming. for very large prefix loads we recommend a dedicated pool pinned with a KV-cache warmed, so initial tokenization and KV upload is amortized. you'll see me show the console where we pin models and set autoscale policies.
[01:25] Jordan Lee: also worth mentioning, if you go hosted vs dedicated, routing policies can fall back to a cheaper quantized variant if capacity constraints occur. that gives graceful degradation instead of full timeouts.
[01:36] Aisha Khan: and that fallback keeps output quality acceptable? we need to avoid hallucination regressions for analytics summaries.
[01:42] Maya Patel: we run model calibration and quality checks; Optimize suggests quant profiles per workload. i'll show a before/after of a long-context prompt with FP16 vs 4-bit quant and the deltas.

[05:00] Maya Patel: jumping into the console now, screen share, you can see the model route config, here we've pinned a 4xA100 pool for the pilot, autoscale min=2 max=12, burst capacity enabled. note the per-route token SLO settings.
[05:18] Liam Chen: question: can we set region affinity for certain routes? we need EU data residency for some customers.
[05:22] Maya Patel: yes, routing supports region policy and we can restrict to eu-west-1; we also have private deployment options for full on-prem.

[08:45] Jordan Lee: quick aside on telemetry, the console gives per-token latency histograms and token-cost breakdowns; for HL peaks you can export traces to your SIEM or we can push to your datadog endpoint.

[12:10] Maya Patel: API demo: long context example. i'll send a 120k token compressed prefix as a KV snapshot, then send incremental messages. transcription note: sometimes our demo logs show "KV cache" being transcribed as "K V cash" in earlier recordings, ha.
[12:32] Aisha Khan: hah yes we've seen that with fireflies.

[15:00] Maya Patel: ok starting synthetic high TPS: we're sending 4k rps of small generation calls (avg 60 tokens) to a hosted pool and then will shift to dedicated. watch the streaming responses; we'll introduce a backpressure condition by dropping a portion of worker capacity to simulate network congestion.
[15:20] Renee Ortiz: how do you simulate backpressure?
[15:24] Maya Patel: two knobs  reduce worker processes or throttle network egress, and we also can lower the concurrency per worker which forces the runtime to queue requests, you'll see the streaming chunk delays.
[15:40] [SYSTEM NOISE] Speaker 3: (inaudible)
[16:05] Maya Patel: starting load now... ok at 1k rps the 95th percentile tokens/sec is steady, at 3k small tail starts to show, at 4k rps we see increased queueing, streaming chunks arrive with jitter, and we trigger our backpressure policy.
[16:25] Jordan Lee: note the backpressure policy here we try to maintain small partial-chunk flushes to keep latency reasonable, and when the queue > threshold we prioritize short tail requests or fallback to a lower-cost quantized model.
[16:38] Liam Chen: do you ever drop streaming connections or just delay? our SREs are worried about client SDKs hanging.
[16:44] Maya Patel: the runtime has configurable timeouts per route; default is 60s for active generation but you can lower it. if a stream stalls we surface a specific backpressure event and can send a partial result + status code so SDKs can retry idempotently.

[22:00] Jordan Lee: quick security check we support SAML SSO for console access, RBAC for routes, audit logs for every request, and CMEK via your KMS provider. anything else on security?
[22:15] Aisha Khan: do you provide audit-level request payload redaction? customer PII needs to be trimmed before logs persist.
[22:22] Maya Patel: yes we have configurable scrubbers and the option to disable payload retention entirely for dedicated/private installs. we'll include the config in the security pack.

[28:40] Maya Patel: back to timeouts: there's a difference between client-level connection timeouts and server-side generation timeouts. server-side we can return a 503 with a structured error explaining whether it was a model call timeout, backpressure eviction, or hardware failure. that helps instrumentation.
[29:02] Renee Ortiz: can we see the structured error schema?
[29:05] Maya Patel: yes i'll paste the schema after the call; it's in our developer docs and the Optimize console surfaces common errors mapped to remediation steps.

[33:55] Maya Patel: demoing long-context accuracy: first example with FP16, we run a 120k-token prompt referencing prior events, generation aligns with expected summary, latency ~1.2s per response chunk. second example with 4-bit quant shows small quality drift on nuanced instructions but 2x throughput.
[34:20] Aisha Khan: that tradeoff is helpful. for our analytics we can tolerate small drift on summarization but not on classification outputs. can you pin a subset of routes to FP16?
[34:29] Jordan Lee: yes route-level model variants are supported; you can pin sensitive routes to FP16 dedicated pools while letting batchable summary routes use quantized models.

[40:10] Maya Patel: now showing the SDK behavior when a streaming chunk is delayed the JS SDK emits onDelta events with a backpressure flag; sample code shows retry semantics and idempotency token usage.
[40:30] Liam Chen: about idempotency, do you recommend unique tokens per user-turn or per request?
[40:34] Maya Patel: per request for retries; for multi-turn we recommend a session id plus per-request idempotency token to dedupe.

[45:50] Jordan Lee: circling back to economics Optimize will run your traffic traces, propose batching window sizes and quantization profiles; we usually see 20-40% token-cost reduction for mixed workloads. for pure high-TPS small responses, batching helps less but autoscaling and dedicated pools drop unit cost.
[46:12] Aisha Khan: what's typical pilot cost for a 48h benchmark?
[46:16] Jordan Lee: depends on pinned capacity; for your projected peaks we can give an estimate in the worksheet, i'll include committed reserved pricing and a short-term burst plan.

[50:00] Renee Ortiz: a practical question if a streaming timeout occurs and the SDK retries, how do you avoid double-counting tokens?
[50:08] Maya Patel: our billing uses idempotency markers for retries; we mark partial-chunk refunds for evicted calls in certain cases and our billing export flags retried tokens separately. we'll share the billing export sample.

[51:30] Aisha Khan: ok this is super helpful. quick logistics we want Redwood to run a synthetic test using our trace and then a pilot environment where we pin capacity for 48h.
[51:40] Jordan Lee: agreed. next steps: we'll send the pricing worksheet and SOC2/KMS docs, Maya will share the synthetic test configs and the structured error schema, and we'll schedule the pilot kickoff Aug 24.
[51:54] Liam Chen: can you also include a Datadog integration example? that helps our SREs.
[52:00] Maya Patel: yup will include.
[52:05] Jordan Lee: any final questions?
[52:09] Aisha Khan: no, thanks everyone, we will review the docs and get back to schedule the kickoff.
[52:16] Renee Ortiz: thanks, bye.
[52:20] Jordan Lee: thanks all, bye.

End of recording.
